projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Gilbert Arbiso, Jr. was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: This is an interview with Mr. Gil Arbiso, Jr.; and I'm going to have him give his address and so on in just a moment. He's a crew member of the Battleship U.S.S. South Dakota. The interview was conducted by Arthur Huseboe on July 6th, 2001 at the Ramkota Hotel in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, during a reunion of the crew of the battleship. And now if you'll just read your name and address, Gil.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah for the record my name is Gilbert called "Gil" for better presentation Arbiso, Jr., and I come from the city of Stanton, California, in Orange County; right next to Disneyland.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Your age when you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: 18. And how come you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I do have... it's kind of a long story but I had an older brother in the Marine Corps; I had a brother in the Army. He was in Patton's Third Army, and though I was an _____ undergraduate in high school. I graduated before everybody else so I could join the Navy, so that I could make it threesome, but my mother tried put a halt to it and she said, "No, you don't have to go." And I remember my mother crying, and I said, "No, Mom. Look. Everything's going to fine." And so I ended up going to San Diego. And the funny part is I've learned something out of life is that you never go against your mother's wishes. So when I got to San Diego, they process a whole crew, and I was the last guy. And it took everything in my power, whatever, to convince those guys that even though I wasn't five feet tall because every time they'd tell me to measure up to the wall, I was standing on my tippytoes. You know, and he says, "You're a determined little cuss, aren't you?" And I says, "Yes, sir. I want to go in the Navy." And that's all they could get out of me, "I want to go in the Navy."

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: I thought about Mother and all that. So, anyway, finally I think instead of one medical staff there was about there was about one here, four over there and they was trying to find out and I could just sense what the conversation was all about. "You know that little sucker is " They pushed me through. I wasn't quite five feet tall. Seriously, maybe, like a quarter of an inch or something. And so anyway, by the time they issued me my clothes; my pants clearly was too long; and I said, "Well, don't you have any smalls?" He said, "Son, that's the smallest we got." I had to roll my pant leg up and my sleeves were too long. I says, "How am I going to walk in these things? They're too big." And he says, "Well, do the best you can." I had to stuff them. And so anyway, got to the barracks, and everybody is there. And I says, "Did you make it, kid?" And he says, "Yeah, why not? We got to win this war. Can't win it unless you have someone who knows what they are going to do."

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: But by the time that it got evening, and they have lights out maybe at nine clock. Nine o'clock comes lights out, and I found myself I cried all night. I wanted to go home; I was homesick. I never... I had never been away from home. I cried when I said I cried all night, I cried. And some of the older fellas said, "Look, son. You can't get out and can't go home. You're in the Navy now." They said, "We'll take care of you. Don't worry, tomorrow will be a different day." Well, ______ my time at school.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You told me you heard a few other guys crying?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, well, you know, after you've cried all night and you're dried out and everything, and you're kind of tired from crying so darn long, you kind of come to a halt, and you listen the rest of the young kids were crying, too. They wanted to go home, too. Sorry kids you can't go now; you're in the Army now. But, anyway, as it turned out, probably the best thing that happened to me in my life, and I could probably say for a lot of other kids that come back. But you know in school, I had been in the band all the time. I could march; I could drill, _______, right, left, do turnabouts and everything; so I ended up being the right guy for the company. Yeah, the right guy is usually the little guy, put him in front of all these big guys. And then you run down to the last guys; you set the pace for the little guys in the back.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So, what happened I had... probably a lot of fellas come out of Tennessee, Kentucky and all that, and those suckers always stepped up, knocked my shoes off, stopped stopped the whole company. And so it was after awhile he got so wrapped up in that. But you know when we graduated from the end of at the end the indoctrination and everything and the training, we had won the pennant for drilling, and so anyway

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Well, I was the guy down there in my company in the artillery, you know, and I did this with the flag, you know. But I was tall and I'm 6'2".

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, that was what my mother used to tell my sisters and my brothers now this guy is going to be 6'4". And, but, you know, I'm still waiting to grow to 6'4". You know, I figured being an accountant she was, wanted to lie to my sister or my brother. I figured 64 inches would be right because right now, I think the tallest I got was 5'4". Well, I cheat a couple of inches so I could come up with the 5'4". That would be 64 inches.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Where did you go for training?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: San Diego. San Diego Training Center.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: How long was that?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: We was this is at the height before we started going to bombard all the islands and all, this is when the heighth of the war really started, and they needed men. But I already had three or four weeks of training, and that's how

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You told me that.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, and it's they were pushing us through fast. I found myself going to, to Pearl Harbor, and got to Pearl Harbor and...

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Remember what month it was then when you got to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Early enough to hit the Marshall Islands.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So we started in the Marshall Islands, and I went from there. We went to Saipan, the Marianas.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You were part of the socalled "Marianas Turkey Shoot."

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: We were the focal point.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: See, the Battleship South Dakota was really the flagship for Andrew Halsey, so that was his flagship; that's what it was built for. And so I wasn't aware that when I went from Pearl Harbor to the islands to catch the ship, I was assigned to the South Dakota. And when I first came aboard, I have to laugh because I could see the expression on the fellas that looked and said, "Gee, we must be losing the war." [LAUGHING] No, but, you ever see a _____?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I know what those are.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: I used to be a mile runner in school. I was on the boxing team; between my two brothers and myself, we had the high school championship for nine straight years. Good athletes in my... My older brother was the captain of the varsity track team. We so were all athletic, pretty wellbuilt. So, when I'm walking up the gangplank [LAUGHING] "Look at the little guy underneath there." And some guy says, "Gee, God, I mean, what are the sending us? Boy, we must be losing the war." I was so darn small. And you know the one thing that impressed me also, that I'll never forget, is that the first fella I ran into was a guy by the name of _____. He was from New Orleans. He was tattooed all over. Big, tall. He was a young fella but he was a lot older than I was. Put his arms around, "Now, this is my chicken." Now what these guys said was nobody mess with the guy. Don't give him a bad time. Don't pick on him and all that. I'm going to defend him. He's I'm going to train this guy.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Good for him.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Because the older guys would look after the young kids; or the younger fellas anyway.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Where were you? Where was the ship stationed when you went aboard? Where was it located?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: In the Marshall Islands.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: In the Marshall Islands someplace.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: We had a guy called _____, that was the Navy that was Navy ____. At that point, that's all the battleships and whatever. That's what we used for that. Later on, we moved to another island called Ulithi, which was a lot bigger.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Ulithi. I've heard of that. Now, were you assigned what was your assignment onboard ship? Were you on some of the guns?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, no. I couldn't reach a gun. They couldn't use me there. But after I looked at when I first came aboard, I guess they looked what do we do with this guy? I never swabbed a deck. I don't know what it is now. No, but they put me up in the conning towers as a lookout. And then after they read my you know, I could type; I knew office machines and all that. They stuck me in the supply office.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: And for the rest of the war, I became a shore keeper. And I used to take care of the title ledgers. I was fairly welleducated at that time. I mean, I was a little advanced for myself. So I'd requisition from Pearl Harbor or ships at sea, you know, materials. We had to seize I'd have to forward the personal belongings of whoever got

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, that was a sad part of it.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: I'm sure it was.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: And at times I'd help disperse the crew and all that. But I was always in the supply. As a matter of fact, that's where I slept, in the supply office. I had a bunk and everything. So, I was welltaken care of.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Were you was there an office complex? There's a pay master and you and all together in one area?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, the supply office was a contained office where we had all the equipment, title ledgers. And I used to take care of the nonexpendable items in case, you know, something happened to the propellers or the heavy equipment. And I'd inventory all that stuff. But most of my time was, you know, everyday routine was in that office. And that... and then if I typed requisitions requesting supplies, material, whatever it was, I'd go down to the the Commanding Officer, the Supply Officer, and either have to get him out of bed or whatever. "Commander, I need your signature." The guy was always in bed, it seemed. We were in thick of battle; I guess he was always in bed. But, anyway

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: What about other supplies, like medical supplies and so on, was there like big

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, that came directly to, because directly from the medical department. If they needed morphine or something like that then, you know, you got to be pretty, pretty much familiar with the medicines and types and what have you. They took care of that.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: So they had regular pharmacists onboard?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, we had a regular hospital onboard. And, but with me is that most of my work was administrative because I was good at the machines and type and all that.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Would they have a extra propeller or two onboard the ship?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: No, no, no. Did you see the propellers out

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Cause there's one just arrived here.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: That came from the Washington, D.C., Navy Yard. I was down there for the Inauguration, and we went down there to take look at it.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: So if you needed a propeller, you'd be

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, I'd be the one to type the requisition, but you know in a case like that it had to be very critical. You need a propeller; you don't it's an emergency thing.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, I know.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Even the Admiral had to be concerned about getting the ship on time.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Now, that was on battle stations when I first went aboard they assigned me to right underneath the Captain's Bridge. You got a starboard, which is the right side. Port, there are magazines. And those magazines, they have ammunition for the forty millimeters. They come in clips. And so we're on our way to Saipan. We got attacked by kamikazes. We bombarded the island and everything. So we'd put the clips in the shoot, and outside, the hammers would pull out and they'd be firing all the time.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: So you were helping to supply ammunition for the forty millimeters?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. Except in the this big explosion. We heard the noise, and all that, but we had no idea what was happening because we were enclosed in the magazine. And so after awhile, there was the Chief _____ mate, Chief Sneed (ph), who was from Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and he'd been regular Navy. And there was some other personnel, they were regular Navy. They had experience. But for the rest of us young kids, we'd look up and we were looking to see what the reaction I mean, you're all confused and what have you. Then you could see little smoke or something coming through. And I says, "Smoke?" So, we'd all start panicking. Someone said, suggested, why don't we just open the hatch, the door to the magazine, and see what's happening? And so they did that, and first thing was, was all kinds of liquid coming in, but it was all red. All these guys had been killed, blown over the side and all that. So, and then, that was the time to be a little concerned. But what we saw was that if you looked at where the bomb went in, you could see the bottom of the magazine. And you could see a figure that within a few inches or so, if that had hit, made an impact, all that magazine would have blown up.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Would have gotten you, too.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yep. So, anyway

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: So that was a Japanese bomb that came?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, we got hit.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Where was that? At Saipan?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, Saipan.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: From a Japanese plane?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Five hundred pound bomb.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Five hundred pound bomb.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So, the only thing is, and I tell everybody, from then on, I became a Christian. You know why I became a Christian? Because I learned prayer aboard a battleship. Now if you had asked me these questions six years ago

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: you told me that.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: I'd be crying right now.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You couldn't talk about it.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Lot of emotion.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: A lot of good men were

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So, anyway, the they have twenty millimeters also along the side of the ship. I mean, it's just like in the movies.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: But anyway, you don't have time to be scared. You're so busy to what they've been I can see where the training comes in, discipline, what have you.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So here comes that [GUNSHOT SOUNDS], you know. There's all these guns, and there was a young kid, Earhart (ph), from Iowa, blond, not much bigger than I was, but he was chunky. And I says, "Okay, Earhart." I picked up a can and put it in, and I said, "Fire!" And he says, "I can't reach it." The harness because they put we were both short like that. I said, "Here, move out of the way." I fired it, but I was firing tracers. That thing was coming, firing at us, and we didn't have any sense to duck or anything like that. We were firing, we were in the middle of whatever. So, anyway, you go back and think about it, and I says, dear Lord, thank you. I just my prayers were, "Lord, I want to be let me get to be 21."

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Did somebody else take over the gun then?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: No, no, no. We did it but by that time we shot all those planes down.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah. What kind of a plane was it? Do you know?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Just a regular kamikaze plane.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: A Zero?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, a Zero is what it was. It just a it's the same kind of plane that dropped the bomb. And so, anyway, you're so involved and so preoccupied and you look at and you have no idea what's happening because everything's happening so fast.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So it's just like in the movies. So after you think about. It's just like in the movies. After you think about it, you're so gosh, we could have been killed. So then after the sounded allclear, we're all in the, you know, we have to pick up the fellas, the damage, and everything. And what a lot of us picked up was this guy, Linder (ph). God, that was we knew it was him because of the tattoos. The guy that was going to look after me and I was, God, it's just and I was, you're in shock most of the time. You were in shock.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: How many were killed at the time? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Quite a few because I remember we buried them at sea. And I just, and anyways, some of those things, I can't really talk about.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: No. That's you know, when you're picking up the arm of one of your best friends. That's there's no way you can describe that.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: They were just really torn to pieces. You know, no head, no nothing. You don't think about it before you sit there and your bunk after that. And the funny part about it we hadn't eaten all day...

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Timeout.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Timeout.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: I get a little emotional.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, well, that's all right. That's about as hazardous as any action that you went through? Was Saipan

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, we was always under attack. You ever see in the movies like the locusts, that you can't see the light because there are so many?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: That's what it was like with the planes. There were so many. The Japanese, they threw everything at us. I mean, every plane they could muster was up. Sometimes it was 200, 250. I mean there were so many planes, you couldn't count them. And so, anyways, that's where it gets it's pretty hard to for an individual to look at, to go back and to reconstruct that. I could never do that. I'm too emotional. I just couldn't.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You were at the Marianas campaign, the socalled "turkey shoot"?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Where a lot of the combat was carried on by F6Fs?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, no. We had F4Fs, too.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: See, I was a lookout. I knew the Japanese Bettys and all these types because of the contours. And we were trained what to look for. And so anyway, you learned the planes, you see a plane fly. And that's what I see a Betty, there's a Zero. And our ships, we have to learn

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: the fighters from the _____ from the dive bombers. We had to know all that. And you know the silhouettes, and you can tell from a distance what they were. But it was, you know, you go back and you can tell your... I never could tell my family, my kids. Because and they would go to their mother, how come Dad never, I see it on the History Channel how come he never talks about? The South Dakota was on there. One time, one of my boys, he says, "Dad, look at here, Dad." I says, "Yeah, Rodney, I was I'm right in there. We were in the middle of all that." Just I mean, we were in the middle of all that.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Well, there were a lot of Japanese planes shot down at that battle, both on, I think, was it on Guam where they had a big airbase?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: All through the Pacific; I mean, the China Seas, we were always under attack. Don't forget we had taken Guadalcanal, taken all these other islands back, and the Japanese were now kind of desperately _______+ throwing everything. They were trying to sink the fleet.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Well, the Marianas are a lot closer to Japan than the Solomon Islands. I mean, you're getting up into Japanese territory. Were you in on the bombardment of Japan at all?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We were still aboard. We bombarded, shelled the coast of Japan. I don't know I don't know whose idea that was but we got close enough to hit the islands. Yeah, seriously. And nobody said anything about it. _____+ but probably the Admirals themselves. God, you got to do something, running around being scared all the time. We did. We shelled the coast of Japan even before the war was over.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Uhhuh.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: But you remember that, then, at that time we're talking about you know, the ships at sea, we were shelling Atenyun. Atenyun (ph) was the island where they basically established to ply the fortresses that would go bomb Japan. And that bomb that the Indianapolis carried well, we didn't know at that time; everything was top secret. And would you believe that the Indianapolis, after it delivered the bomb, got sunk?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: It did?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: They had already delivered the

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Kamikaze? Or submarine?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: It got torpedoed. Yeah, submarine. See, all of these movies, some of these guys have done a lot of research and all that.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure, sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: They found that that how the bomb got there, and who participated. But anyway, all that was top secret. My... my battle station the reason I had learned a lot is because I was in what you call CIC, Combat Information Center, way down in the hold. We had all the radar, all this the TBS, Transmission Between Ships. I used to type all that information in code.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: And I could receive and respond. And if the Admiral said social time the fleet will ship, and the whole fleet would ship.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Is that broadcast in code?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, yeah, in code. But the ships themselves had code names. You know the cargo, cargo, this is so and this and that _____+. Carry out this and that. It was all transmissions in code.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: I suppose the

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: You could see, I could see all the ships at sea like this on the big plot. We knew where they were at. And that's where they used to have me there then. And then, I'd be down in where they fire the computers. You could fire the guns, you could fire the guns from that ship from three different locations, in case something was damaged, you could what they called fire control you could fire down in the bottom. And they had... the 16inch guns could be fired with a, just a pistol. Like this and that. _____+

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: By radar? They could aim them by radar?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: And then were there Fire Direction Officers?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, we didn't have that much radar at that time. That was fairly new at that time. But the radio in the estimated range and stuff like that the computers will digest that and they say, "Fire," and that's all they have to do is fire. And then there is another one in case the ship is disabled from a different part of the ship that can serve the ship and whatever. So, it's... well, that's why your a lot of times the general public, you can't tell the general public everything because first thing you know it's the killer. They undermine a lot of things.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Did you have reporters onboard the ship at all?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: No, no. Come on, we were fighting a war. We're not... the other one is that, that it's my personal feeling, observation is that I have been a proponent of military conscript is that ______ if nothing else. At the age of 18, at least 18 months, a year and a half of don't want to build another Germany or Nazi Germany. And just the fact that, you know, we fought everybody in the world. We fought Japan, China, and Germany, Italy and all these foreign countries. The one thing is those wars have never came to our shores where our kids have been, you know, kicked around and tortured and everything and our women raped and all that. We haven't had that. And look at now, modern times, now, some of these Asians countries have the mechanics the... they have the answer to how you can get a missile over here and do destruction. And this is why it's very important you know, I'm not one to advocate being in war. I'm not a warmonger and all that. But I says a safe nation is strong nation. So, I... I was very instrumental in voicing my opinion that during the Clinton years, they didn't want a big Army, they wanted social programs. Well, social programs are good to a certain point. And I realize that going to school, and I talked to a lot of my professors and everything, and well, it gets a little political a lot of times. And, you know, the main thing is that we want a safe country. And if you've been exposed to areas how these wars are conducted, all the damage they do, and all the grief and all the heart you can't go to a family ____ you know, like the Solomons Their four sons or five sons went down with the ship. I mean, that's horrible.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: That's a terrible thing.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: You know, my two brothers, we all came back pretty heavily decorated.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Uhhuh.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: If you read my thing, I've got 11 Battle Stars, and that doesn't include the battle of the ______+.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: 11 battle stars.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Two or three more... one each for the Battle of the Philippine Seas, the second was for Leyte Gulf, that's the second battle of the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Leyte Gulf, off yeah. Where there were three Japanese forces?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: South, middle, and the north. You were up north?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, we were in the middle. And all we were chasing the Japanese fleet. But, and we had a meeting, just a reunion in Biloxi, Mississippi, and got to some of the guys from the old battleships, and they just hated Halsey, they says. Because they felt that Halsey had left them unprotected. This is a small _____ Jeep Carriers. The Jeep Carriers carried, not as large as the Enterprise or these other big ships. But they carried, they ferried planes and everything to them. So, they were and then, the old battlewagon was then and so... they felt safe because we had the rest the fleet. But you know, we had we always carried, like, the South Dakota, the Indiana. They were all the new ships. The Wisconsin, the Independence, the Washington, and then we had carried about maybe four, five, six carriers, big carriers, destroyers, cruisers. And they all they all congregate and it's all one defense. One and so anyway, when Halsey started to move through the San Bernita Straits (ph) to the South China seas following the Navy Fleet, well, these guys got attacked over there. They harbor that bitterness, you know. I says, now, wait a minute. We're fighting a war, you can't really condemn the guy. But he was determined to get the Japanese fleet. But, somehow or other but the old battlewagons were there to protect them, you know. And some of the battle wagons still had fourteeninch guns; we had sixteeninch guns.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: But you know it's nice to be alive. Seriously.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. How are we doing? Well, we're doing all right for time. I was going to ask you about some specific things, like, what did you what was your reaction to the threat of submarines? I mean, submarines were always around. Was that a concern for you?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: It's always been a concern. But you see, a battlewagon, they have armor below the waterline. But it's only so good, only so thick; right? But it within, within a fleet you also the first thing you guard is your aircraft carriers because they've got all the planes and everything.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure, sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: And outside the line, there's the battlewagons, and outside the battlewagons is your cruisers; and then outside the cruisers, you have destroyers; smaller ships; destroy escorts. And they have, they have pickets, picket ships. Everything is one big network and all that. So you're always testing the waters for what's around you. So you feel pretty comfortable, not comfortable, but, you know, fairly safe. If you're going to be safe.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Part of your duty was helping sea communications among

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, see, this is only on battle station when we're under attack. I'd go down to my station, put on my phones and all that, I could see all the fleet and everything and I whatever communications came on, I'd type it, give to the people in charge and, you know, the captains and the... And so they would they would make those decisions anyway. But most of mine was just keep track of where the fleet's at, and if there was any instructions, I'd type. Receive and transmit, that's what I would do.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: How about bad weather?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, bad weather was we had two typhoons. Typhoons that, I don't know if you... it's unbelievable what happens, how strong water can be in a typhoon. You weren't allowed on the top deck. It was water doors. And somewhere, I forget, off in the Pacific, we lost three battleships, destroyers. That were, they were listing so bad and the water was so rough they tipped over ninety degrees. They took water to the front and that's all it took to take them down. Anyway. So you know it's... it's pretty hard to describe, I mean, because you know water has a lot of force. But our ship, as big it was, I never seen a ship go up and come down and it pounds. I mean, the whole ship would shake. But we had two typhoons of that caliber. And it was strong. And in history, there was two of the strongest typhoons that they'd experienced.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You didn't have any way of knowing, predicting that they were coming. No way to hideout.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: No. There there's no time for experimentation, stuff like that. You fight what you run into, what it is. But anyway, I think I'm a great believer now of training. Training, and we would wonder why you see, at that time we'd go through an obstacle course and I'd been a mile runner in school, and it was the older fellas that I felt sorry. ______+ God, here's a poor guy. He's 35 40years old, having a hard time going over this.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: And but, you know, that the age you can, just like a rabbit, and I'd run. I was a mile runner, an athlete. You're always in condition, what have you. But that's why I say, that's why I say, it's always good to have that kind of training. And the other one that I've always been very concerned is that if you have these guys in some kind of training, you know, it doesn't have to be military training. Just discipline. You need to have them off the streets. In this world, we have the big battle now. We got a bigger battle right here with drugs and what have you. I just... I was I always worked on the in town at the Boys Club and the Charlotte Boys Club. And my house, garage, and all that, out of our own pockets and all that. Now we have a large Boys now it's Boy and Girls Club. We had to include the girls, too.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure, sure.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So, and you know, it's to me I have been doing well my life. And I thank the good Lord that I got to be 21. I've been ready to go ...

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: It's the amazing that the South Dakota was in service such a short time. Three, four years is all.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Here's something that the average individual doesn't understand, everything in this in our society involves politics. You go to the schools, you got a political faction; you go to the Boy Scouts, you got a political faction; the PTA everything has got, is politicized. But at the time that we anchored in Yokosuka and then see, the Missouri doesn't come into the war until later on. But don't forget, Truman was our President, and so, what the heck is the Secretary of Navy? It's no, no. Oh God, I had his name. Anyway, he they said, well, you know, Truman is from Missouri. Let's honor the President. Well, the President, I says... well, all our veteran guys that have been solid Navy and we had gone through all this. Why would you give it to a ship that just you know, glory thing and all that. They were all upset. I didn't care. I wanted to go home. I said, well, you know, I was still crying at that time; I want to go home. I mean, what the hell? I said, I hate to say, well, I hate to be a crybaby. But I mean, but I went through all these things. I mean, it doesn't make me less of a man. But I'm just very emotional. I wanted to go home.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: What did what did the men think about, as it was clear the war was winding down, but what did they think about the next phase, which would be invading Japan? Was there much talk about that?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: You know, about invading Japan, I want to tell you something. All these few years, I've been trying to face to what I've seen and what I went through. Before I wasn't willing to face it, I couldn't to face it. I was but I remember when we anchored at Yokosuka Bay, I went ashore. I was the Supply Office, as a messenger. Me, myself, my five foot stature and they put me ashore, and I had to deliver a message to the Base Commander. And I'm surrounded by... I'll tell you how bad Japan was at that point. I was barely now at this point, I had grown. I had grew up some, right? So, now I'm, I could have been 5'1" or something like that. I looked down and there's all these little guys. Man, I felt like I felt like a HeMan. Walked out, I felt so big. ______+ the Japanese people. I says, all these sailors and soldiers that were so caps and everything, little bitty guys. I never knew that they was that small. I felt, I felt humongous. I mean, I says, leave me here. I'll fight the war all over. But I can't remember where I went to and all that. I just delivered that.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: But I was thinking about before the surrender.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: The surrender?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, in that...

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Well, yeah, they had... they had some assigned some responsibilities of how you were going to take maybe certain men, off the ships and put a unit together. But, you know, you just don't go invade a country. They had already surrendered. What is it to go in there and do?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: You're not going to go harass people.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: No, no, no, no.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: So, anyway, the one thing that was going to be resolved was the agreement to put an end to it and all that. But the flagship was Halsey was already aboard a ship. The surrender was going to be signed aboard the South Dakota. But after these _____+, you know, the Missouri's. And everybody's all upset, all the old guys. Man, I just wanted to come home. I didn't care. But now I go think of it, and that wasn't fair, wasn't fair for the... and then every time we have a meeting in the Missouri, says, yeah, we're sorry. It really should have been signed aboard the Missouri. And so, I was at Pearl Harbor three years ago for the memorial, when they towed the and I went to represent the I got a call from the Admiral in San Diego. Would I represent the ship and the crew? I didn't have time to say, "Well, let me think about it." God, I'd be honored. I said and there was three other guys that were still living representing other ships. We were part of the ceremony. You had diplomates from all over the world, you know, Japan, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, China, everything. And it was broadcast all over to the Armed Forces and everything. We participated. That was it will be three years next September. That was the last time I was aboard the Missouri. Aboard the misery.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: The misery? Yeah. What was the reason for it? Why did they get

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: They towed they made a memorial out of the...

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh. The Arizona?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: No, no, no. It's it's the Missouri. You know, the Battleship Missouri. It's anchored right directly in front of the Arizona or in back of the Arizona. And it's a memorial.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: So you can go through the whole ship?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yep, yep.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: It's kept up and all?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. ______+ and it was assigned to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: That's what should have happened to the South Dakota.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: No. I tell you what, this is where... they were in a hurry to dismantle that ship. They just you know. But if you look the annals of records and the Navy Archives, that ship was the most decorated ship in the fleet. Now be aware that even though we had a carrier with I don't know how many hundreds of planes on there they knocked a lot of planes down. Well, the carrier would probably get credit for all that. But we had, we knocked tons of planes down. Sixty, eighty Japanese planes. We were out there fighting, you know, to save our ship and all that.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: I think I'm hearing the tap for the next guy.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: Okay. Whenever you want to get rid of me.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: I don't want to get rid of you. We got give the next guy a chance to. Anything you want to add, Gil?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Arbiso, Jr.
sp.p: No, no. It's just that... I've been to the reunions since the first one in 1970. And when we at that time there was Nancy Gatts (ph), the Skipper's daughter. Her husband, Andrew ______, who was a neurosurgeon from the Mayo Clinic, which I got to know, love her dearly. Tom Gatts (ph), who was also the Skipper's son, tried to go across the Atlantic in a balloon. And they never found him. They got lost at sea or something. So we got together and we said we were going get together and have a reunion every three years to commemorate the ship, honor the men that didn't make it back. That was the whole concept. But after the third year, we found out that so many people had passed on. So that we moved it to every two years. So, next after '75, we have been meeting every two years. I'm done as far as I'm concerned. I'm glad I fought the war. I'm glad we won the war. But I don't want to see my kids; I've got four sons. They're drug-free, good athletes. And they're very good Christians, by the way. Anyway, and on that note, I end my discussion. I'm going to have breakfast.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: All right.
